product: Audio Speech API — gpt-4o-mini-tts, tts-1, tts-1-hd, plus Custom Voices
recut_note: Re-cut onto the corrected frame after Tom's course correction of 2026-08-26 11:06Z: Welsh is OUT (human-recorded), coverage is counted against the three tiers of languages that actually use TTS, and TTS is a BRIDGE to human recording, so exit cost is scored alongside entry cost. The vendor research below is unchanged and every source citation is the original one; the frame around it is new. Companion dossier: docs/tts-bakeoff/gate-zero-candidates-recut-2026-08-26.md

headline.one_line: Much the widest tier coverage, the best written version-pinning policy, and the only candidate whose contract explicitly assigns Output ownership to us and survives termination — the best bridge among the hosted three, gated behind a sales conversation nobody has had.
headline.tier_coverage: Tier A 9/10 (misses ben — ben_for_eng is LIVE with 20,315 clips). Tier B 10/11 (misses pdc only). Tier A+B+C 40/44 — eleven languages clear of the next best.
headline.discriminator: OpenAI is the only candidate where breadth is a real advantage, and it shows only in Tier C: 40/44 against MiniMax's 31 and Cartesia's 29. On Tier A and Tier B it is level with the field. Its decisive advantages are contractual: Customer 'owns all Output', OpenAI 'assigns to Customer all OpenAI's right, title, and interest' in it, the IP clause survives termination, and OpenAI must delete all Customer Content within 30 days of termination. Its weaknesses are functional: no timestamps at all, a fixed 24 kHz output, no pronunciation control of any kind, and Custom Voices restricted to 'eligible customers' behind sales.
headline.verdict: STRONGEST HOSTED CANDIDATE ON PAPER AND THE EASIEST HOSTED BRIDGE TO LEAVE. The gating action is Tom opening the Custom Voices conversation with OpenAI sales; until that happens the clone route is theoretical. Quality is entirely unmeasured and the pronunciation-control gap is a genuine risk for a pronunciation-teaching product.

sources.title: Text to speech — OpenAI API docs
sources.what_it_established: THE Welsh finding: the supported-language list ends '...Urdu, Vietnamese, and Welsh', with the caveat 'The TTS model generally follows the Whisper model in terms of language support' and that these languages perform well 'despite voices being optimized for English'. Also: models gpt-4o-mini-tts, tts-1, tts-1-hd; 13 built-in voices; the instructions parameter controlling accent, emotional range, intonation, impressions, speed, tone and whispering; and the existence of Custom Voices with a required consent recording, a sample of 30 seconds or less, and a cap of 20 voices per organisation.

sources.title: GPT-4o mini TTS model page
sources.what_it_established: DATED SNAPSHOTS EXIST: gpt-4o-mini-tts-2025-03-20 and gpt-4o-mini-tts-2025-12-15 (current default). Pricing $0.60 per 1M input tokens and $12 per 1M output audio tokens. Rate limits by tier from 500 RPM / 50K TPM (tier 1) to 10,000 RPM / 8M TPM (tier 5). Maximum 2000 input tokens per request.

sources.title: Deprecations — OpenAI API docs
sources.what_it_established: Written notice policy: at least 6 months for generally available models, at least 3 months for specialised variants, as little as 2 weeks for preview models, with safety or compliance able to accelerate. No TTS model currently carries a deprecation notice; gpt-audio and gpt-realtime variants have shutdown dates of 2027-01-20.

sources.title: Create voice consent — API reference
sources.what_it_established: Consent is a first-class API resource with its own endpoints (create/retrieve/update/list voice consents). A consent upload carries a BCP 47 language tag for the phrase (e.g. en-US), a label, and an audio file up to 10 MiB. Custom voice creation requires an audio sample plus a previously uploaded consent recording id, and any divergence from the approved script fails the upload.

welsh_footnote.evidence: The Text to speech guide's supported-language list names Welsh explicitly, as the final entry: '...Turkish, Ukrainian, Urdu, Vietnamese, and Welsh.' It is the ONLY one of the four candidates that names Welsh anywhere. The caveat matters and is quoted here so nobody over-reads the win: 'The TTS model generally follows the Whisper model in terms of language support' — that is a SPEECH RECOGNITION language list borrowed for a synthesis product — and the list is introduced as performing well 'despite voices being optimized for English'.
welsh_footnote.rationale: Survives, and it is the only candidate that survives on documentation rather than on hope. But 'listed' here is a weaker claim than the word suggests, and I would rather say that plainly now than have it discovered in phase 2. The list is inherited from Whisper, which is an ASR model — the ability to TRANSCRIBE Welsh is not evidence of the ability to SPEAK it — and OpenAI's own sentence concedes the voices are optimised for English. The realistic expectation is intelligible Welsh spoken with an anglophone accent, which for a Welsh-teaching course is not a minor blemish but close to a disqualification: SSi's Welsh learners are learning pronunciation from these clips. So the honest position is that OpenAI clears gate zero on paper and the real gate is a listening test. On dialect, OpenAI is in the same place as everyone else — nothing addresses north versus south Welsh — but it is the only candidate with a documented, contractual custom-voice path, so the question 'can a clone of Aran carry north Welsh' is at least askable through a supported product rather than by abusing an undocumented capability. Two caveats on that path: Custom Voices are 'limited to eligible customers' and gated behind a sales conversation, so it is not self-serve and Tom cannot simply sign up; and the approved consent phrases are published in de, en, es, fr, hi, id, it, ja, ko, nl, pl, pt, ru, uk, vi and zh — no Welsh, so Aran and Catrin would record their consent in English.
welsh_footnote.demoted_because: Welsh is done by human recording (cym_n_for_eng / cym_s_for_eng are 96.4% human, the only human-voiced language in the estate). Vendor Welsh support does not decide this evaluation. Kept verbatim because it is the only yardstick we have for a vendor's reach into Welsh, which will matter if the human-recording programme ever needs a synthetic stand-in. The gate_zero verdict inside this block is SUPERSEDED and must not be quoted as a live verdict.

exit_cost.verdict: EASY — the easiest hosted bridge to leave, and the only one where the exit is written down.
exit_cost.score_rationale: OpenAI is the only candidate whose contract assigns Output ownership to the customer, says so in a clause that survives termination, and commits to deleting customer content within thirty days of the agreement ending. That is a real exit, on paper, in advance. What it does not give is any timing data at all and any control over pronunciation — functional costs that fall on us during the crossing rather than at the end of it.

boundary_data.detail: The /v1/audio/speech endpoint returns audio bytes and nothing else; no word timestamps, no phoneme timestamps, no alignment, no flag to request any. Same position as Chatterbox and as xAI today. Consequence for us is the same: the component-splice path in phase8 that cuts sub-word clips on stored word_boundaries cannot be fed from OpenAI output, and boundaries would have to be derived locally with whisper — which unlike Chatterbox we would be paying per character for anyway.

audio_format.containers: mp3 (default), opus, aac, flac, wav, pcm
audio_format.detail: pcm is documented as raw samples at 24 kHz, 16-bit signed, little-endian, headerless. There is no sample-rate parameter — the rate is fixed by the model, unlike Cartesia and MiniMax which both expose 44100.
audio_format.fits_house_master: WITH AN UPSAMPLE, exactly as Chatterbox. 24 kHz means a bandwidth ceiling near 12 kHz that persists after the house 44.1 kHz mp3 master, and it becomes an audible-adjacent question in a part-migrated course where these clips play alongside full-bandwidth human recordings.

licensing_after_we_stop_paying.verdict: GOOD, AND IN WRITING. The best of the four.
licensing_after_we_stop_paying.detail: The OpenAI Services Agreement states that Customer retains all ownership rights in Input and owns all Output, and that 'OpenAI hereby assigns to Customer all OpenAI's right, title, and interest, if any, in and to Output.' That is an assignment, not a licence, so there is nothing to lapse. The agreement's survival clause explicitly enumerates §9 (IP Rights) among the provisions that survive termination or expiry, alongside §11.3 (Effects of Termination) and §11.4 (Survival). Unlike Cartesia there is no subscription-tier condition on commercial use of Output, and unlike MiniMax there is no perpetual grant running the other way. On the narrow question the brief asks — can we keep serving the clips after we stop paying — OpenAI is the only candidate that answers yes on the page.

clone_retirement.mechanism: DELETE /v1/audio/voice_consents/{consent_id}, plus a contractual deletion obligation on termination.
clone_retirement.detail: Consent is a first-class API resource with create, retrieve, update, list and delete endpoints, and a custom voice cannot exist without referencing a consent recording id — so the consent Aran and Catrin give has a place to live AND a documented way to be withdrawn, which no other candidate offers. Behind it sits the Services Agreement commitment that on termination OpenAI 'will delete all Customer Content from its systems within thirty days', subject to legal-retention and abuse exceptions. Retirement is therefore both an API call and a contractual obligation with a stated clock — the strongest position of the four.

gaps: A DELETE endpoint for the custom VOICE itself (as distinct from the consent recording) was not found — the documentation URL for it returned 404 and search surfaced only the voice_consents delete. Whether a custom voice can be deleted independently of its consent record is unverified.

Sample rates for the non-pcm formats (mp3, wav, flac) are not stated in OpenAI's own documentation; 24 kHz is documented for pcm and is the model's native rate, so the others are inferred from it rather than cited.

Custom Voices remain 'limited to eligible customers' behind a sales conversation, so the entire clone path — including everything good about its exit terms — is theoretical until Tom opens that conversation.
Nothing was measured. There is no OpenAI key on this box.

version_pinning: The best written position of the four. Dated snapshots exist and are callable — gpt-4o-mini-tts-2025-03-20 and gpt-4o-mini-tts-2025-12-15, the latter now the default — so a pin is a real thing you name in a request, and the fact that the March snapshot is still live nine months after a newer default shipped is evidence the pins are honoured. Behind it sits an actual published deprecation policy: at least 6 months notice for generally available models, at least 3 months for specialised variants, as little as 2 weeks for previews, with safety or compliance able to accelerate. No TTS model currently carries a deprecation notice. What still does not exist — and does not exist at any vendor — is a written guarantee that the same text plus the same voice plus the same version renders identically next year. A pinned snapshot plus a 6-month notice floor is the closest thing on the market to Azure's behaviour, but it is a notice period, not a determinism promise, and there is no seed to make an individual render reproducible.
cloning_consent: The only candidate with a real consent MECHANISM rather than a clause in the terms — consent is a first-class API resource with create, retrieve, update and list endpoints, and a custom voice cannot be created without referencing a previously uploaded consent recording id. WORDS TOM COULD FORWARD TO ARAN AND CATRIN: OpenAI will not let us create your voice unless you personally record a short consent statement. You read one specific approved phrase, word for word — any deviation from the script and the upload is rejected. The approved phrases are published in sixteen languages, and Welsh is not one of them, so you would record it in English. Separately you provide a voice sample of 30 seconds or less, in mpeg, wav, ogg, aac, flac, webm or mp4, up to 10 MiB, and you tag the consent with its language (en-GB). That is the whole ask: one scripted sentence and half a minute of speech. Our organisation can hold at most 20 custom voices in total, and the consent record stays on file and is retrievable and updatable, so withdrawal has somewhere to live. The catch to be honest about up front: Custom Voices are 'limited to eligible customers' and require a conversation with OpenAI sales — this is not something we can just switch on, and until that conversation happens the whole custom-voice route is theoretical.

controls.seed: Absent. No seed parameter on the speech endpoint.
controls.temperature: Absent. No temperature parameter on the speech endpoint.
controls.other: The distinctive control is instructions — free-text steering of 'accent, emotional range, intonation, impressions, speed of speech, tone, whispering'. Powerful and, for our purposes, dangerous: a natural-language control has no version and no guarantee that the same instruction string maps to the same delivery after a model update, so it is the opposite of repeatability and should be pinned to a fixed string or avoided. Response format and speed are available. NO pronunciation dictionary, NO IPA, NO phoneme tags and NO SSML — you can only ask in English prose for a word to be said differently, which is the weakest pronunciation control of the four. For teaching pronunciation that is a genuine functional gap. Input capped at 2000 tokens per request.

self_host: No. Hosted API only, closed weights, no on-prem offer.
pricing: $0.60 per 1M input tokens and $12 per 1M output audio tokens for gpt-4o-mini-tts. OpenAI's own commonly quoted estimate is roughly $0.015 per minute of audio, which is around $15 per hour of speech and cheap relative to the field. Older tts-1 and tts-1-hd are priced per character on a separate schedule not read in this slice.
rate_limits: Tiered and generous: 500 RPM / 50,000 TPM at tier 1, rising through 2,000/150,000, 5,000/600,000, 10,000/2,000,000 to 10,000 RPM / 8,000,000 TPM at tier 5. Best headroom of the four for an estate-wide re-render. Per-request input is capped at 2000 tokens, so long seeds must be chunked.
gaps: No OpenAI API key on this box. Nothing was rendered or measured; the Welsh claim is a documentation claim and has not been heard.

THE WELSH CAVEAT IS THE FINDING, not a footnote: the language list is inherited from Whisper, a speech-RECOGNITION model, and OpenAI's own text concedes the voices are 'optimized for English'. Welsh being listed does not mean Welsh sounds Welsh. A listening test by a Welsh speaker is the only thing that settles it and it is a phase-2 item.

Custom Voices are 'limited to eligible customers' behind a sales conversation. We do not know whether SSi qualifies, what it costs, or how long approval takes. Tom would need to open that conversation before the clone route is even testable — this is the gating action item on this candidate.
The approved consent phrases exist in 16 languages and Welsh is not among them; Aran and Catrin would consent in English. Minor, but worth them knowing in advance.
No seed and no temperature, so individual renders cannot be made reproducible even with a pinned snapshot.
No pronunciation override of any kind — no lexicon, no IPA, no SSML. The only lever is the instructions free-text field, which is itself unversioned.
The instructions parameter's stability across model updates is unspecified and is a repeatability risk if we come to depend on it.
No Basque (eus) — OpenAI lists Galician and Catalan but not Basque, so SSi's two Basque courses are uncovered here too.
